correctness.rationale: Each vertex in one induced facet is a sink with probability p=2^(1-d). With 2^(d-1) vertices and d-1 ordered neighbors per vertex, the variance is 1-dp; only adjacent sink indicators have negative covariance. Opposite facets use disjoint edges. For adjacent facets the shared vertex can be a sink in both iff all d incident edges point in. The contribution summed over the 2^(d-2) shared vertices is 1/4-2^(-d); the only other overlapping demands are ordered adjacent pairs inside the intersection, giving -(d-2)2^(-d). The sum is positive iff d≥4. At d=2 there are no shared edges; at d=3 conditioning on the sole shared edge leaves independent residual orientations. Reversing that edge preserves each square's conditional sink-count law by reflection, so the mixture is still independent. For the quantitative limit, each intersection vertex supports three mutually exclusive atoms requiring d directions; exterior atoms require d-1. Total atom means are 3/4, 3/4 and 1/4, with common atoms counted in both coordinates. The same-or-neighbor vertex neighborhoods have ≤3(d+1) indices, so b1≤(7/4)·3(d+1)·2^(1-d). Distinct same-vertex atoms are incompatible, and adjacent vertices' requirements overlap in at most one Bernoulli edge; b2≤2b1 and b3=0. The published AGG process bound 2(2b1+2b2+b3) uses doubled TV, yielding ordinary TV ≤63(d+1)2^(-d). The grouping map contracts TV and gives the specified independent Poisson marks, hence the joint no-sink limit e^(-7/4). The opposite pair has independent marginals with the same Poisson(1) limit. value.rationale: A natural joint statistic shows a finite independence threshold invisible to either facet marginal and persistent dependence even while each count becomes Poisson. The exact common intensity distinguishes adjacent from opposite facets, for example e^(-7/4) versus e^(-2) for joint absence. The classification and quantitative joint approximation are useful benchmarks for dependence among local optima on cube faces, without requiring the TV prefactor to be sharp.
